input:
In this example, we will calculate the available net positive suction head for a pump that draws condensate from an open tank at atmospheric pressure, 101.3 kPa.

The available net positive suction head, denoted $NPSH_a$, is the margin by which the pressure at the pump suction exceeds the vapour pressure of the liquid, expressed in terms of head of the pumped liquid. The vapour pressure at the pumping temperature is 2.3 kPa. The static lift, the height the liquid is raised from the tank surface to the pump centreline, is 1.1 m, and the friction loss in the suction line is 0.8 m. Both the lift and the friction loss consume a portion of the available pressure margin, and both therefore have to be subtracted from it, as set out in the following relation:

$$NPSH_a = \frac{P_{atm} - P_v}{\rho g} - h_{lift} - h_f$$

In this relation, $P_{atm}$ denotes the pressure acting on the liquid surface in the tank, $P_v$ denotes the vapour pressure at the pumping temperature, $\rho$ denotes the liquid density, $g$ denotes the acceleration due to gravity, $h_{lift}$ denotes the static lift, and $h_f$ denotes the suction-line friction loss. The pressure terms are divided by $\rho g$ so that every term is expressed in metres of liquid, allowing the terms to be added and subtracted directly. Substituting the values gives $NPSH_a$ = 8.2 m.

This figure is a margin rather than a duty: 8.2 m is the head available above vaporisation under the stated conditions. Its proper use is as a comparison. The pump's required NPSH at the duty flow is obtained from the vendor curve, and the available head must exceed the required head by a suitable margin. A pump whose required NPSH comes close to 8.2 m at the duty flow would not be acceptable for this service, no matter how closely the two figures might appear to agree, because the vapour pressure, the lift, and the friction loss all shift with changing operating conditions.
